meta.title: Meta's Dina Powell McCormick: The Case for Data Centers, Backlash, AI Job Boom & Meta's Future
meta.speakers: Dina Powell McCormick (Meta president & vice chair); guests Sheldon (Richland Parish superintendent), Susan (Louisiana economic development secretary); hosts Jason Calacanis, Chamath Palihapitiya, David Sacks
meta.thread_line: 5 threads · Richland Parish: a data center pays teachers $50K checks · Meta's community compact and the backlash · a paid trades pipeline (America's Workforce Academy) · the teen-use settlement and new defaults · glasses, Muse and open-source superintelligence

snapshot: Meta's largest data center, in rural Richland Parish, Louisiana, sent school sales-tax collections up as much as ~260% — certified teachers got a ~$50K check this June vs. ~$10K the year before.
Data centers poll around -80 in the US; Dina's answer is a compact: pay your own power and drive rates down, use less water, fund teachers and first responders, and let communities opt out.
Louisiana calls Meta's Entergy deal the prototype: Meta paid for its own generation, grid upgrades, resilience and even hurricane storm costs.

America's Workforce Academy — paid 4-5 week training with a guaranteed data-center job — drew 40,000 applicants in four months, graduated 250 with 90% retention; the building-trades unions now back only pro-data-center candidates.
Jason presses on Meta's record teen-harm settlement; Dina rejects the premise and cites a 52-AG deal: under-18s capped at 2 hours a day, off at night, 1 hour if YouTube, TikTok and Snap join.
Meta glasses: 10 years of engineering, conversation focus and translation, and an unplanned breakout use case with blind veterans.
On Dario's essay: safety is paramount, but Zuckerberg believes distributing superintelligence to 3.6B daily users makes society more stable — Meta just shipped the first American open-source model.

themes.status: META'S FIRST IN LOUISIANA · GROUNDBREAKING DEC 2024
themes.title: Richland Parish: Meta's biggest data center turned into $50K teacher checks
themes.lead: Louisiana's superintendent and economic-development secretary show how a data center's sales tax flowed straight to teacher pay in a parish that had been losing people.
bullets: First contact with Meta in summer 2024 at the local community college — "The game has changed"; groundbreaking December 2024.
School sales-tax collections, normally +5-10%, jumped to ~60% and peaked around **+260%** as construction staffing rose; the school board collects 51% of parish taxes.
A 1-cent and half-cent sales tax go to salaries by law: December 2025's check doubled (~$4K → ~$8K), and June's certified-staff check hit ~$50K vs. ~$10K a year earlier — about $45K net more.
Before Meta, average wages were ~$36-38K; young people left; now caterers went from 40 meals to 400 a week, teacher recruiting is easy, and people are moving home.
Communication must reach "the least informed person in the community," not the most informed.

Louisiana's governor signed an executive order setting a framework for large-load users; with a sales-tax exemption, the state now "gets to be choosy" — "not saying no" but "yes and." Rural parishes are calling asking for the next one.

quote.text: I just sat there and I said, the game has changed.

themes.watch: Meta produced the video and brought the officials; both guests describe their own deal. Dina says the teacher bonuses were a state law, not Meta's idea.

names.name: Meta (META)
names.blurb: Largest data center in Richland Parish, LA; the state's prototype deal.

themes.status: DATA CENTERS POLL ~ -80 IN THE US
themes.title: Meta's community compact vs. the data-center backlash
themes.lead: Jason lists the real grievances; Dina says the industry has communicated badly, but a compact on power, water and local benefits answers them — and adversaries may be fanning the backlash.
bullets: Jason's list: pollution, rising electricity bills, water, noise, ugly buildings — "not journalism... it's facts" from communities that got bad neighbors.
Water: on former farmland, Meta chose a costlier, more efficient cooling system that uses *less* water than the farm did.

Power: Louisiana has ~32,000 miles of gas pipelines; under Meta's deal with **Entergy**, it paid for its own generation, grid upgrades, resilience and hurricane storm costs from day one — before any presidential or governor order.

Meta's compact: pay your own electricity and push rates down; AI-driven water tech; tax surplus to teachers and first responders; small-business growth — and if a community doesn't want a data center, "they get to choose."

Dina, a former deputy national security advisor: Senate intel chairs Cotton and Warner believe adversaries are stoking the backlash — "if you wanted to stop America right now... this is exactly what you would try to do."
Sacks: the federated republic means "some states are going to be idiots and they're going to lose"; Meta also cites Texas and Ohio sites.

quote.text: I don't think that our industry has done a good job communicating. Just flat out.

themes.watch: Dina can't confirm the foreign-influence evidence ("I can't comment on that"); she's describing a position that serves Meta's buildout.

names.name: Entergy (ETR)
names.blurb: Louisiana utility; Meta paid for its own generation and grid costs.

themes.title: America's Workforce Academy: paid training, guaranteed jobs, unions on board
themes.lead: Meta couldn't find enough fiber technicians, so it built a fast-track, paid program that guarantees a data-center job — and is pulling in unions, rivals and other employers.
bullets: Bottleneck: welders, pipefitters, electricians and especially fiber technicians; Meta built the curriculum with partners including CBRE.
A 4-5 week program with safety/OSHA and "job site ready" certification; Meta guarantees graduates a job on its sites, and the credential is portable.
The unlock: trainees are paid what the job pays during training — waitresses, Uber drivers and home-health aides can't afford unpaid courses.
Results: ~40,000 applied in four months, 250 graduated, 90% retention; Sacks' estimate is 500,000 open trade jobs over the next couple of years. Pittsburgh welders earn $100-120K.

Deliberately not branded Meta; partners include the Associated Builders and Contractors, and Ruth Porat's Google-led workforce alliance (with Larry Fink's BlackRock), which Meta is joining — "we compete on models... not on people."
GM's Mary Barra asked for 1,000 workers; NABTU's Sean McGarvey and the building trades now oppose the backlash and will back only pro-data-center candidates.

quote.text: We might compete on models and products, but we don't want to compete on people.

themes.watch: Jason jokes that AI-displaced developers can retrain as electricians — the panel doesn't address how many of these roles outlast construction.

themes.title: The teen-harm settlement: Jason's fastball vs. Meta's new defaults
themes.lead: Jason calls Meta's settlement second only to tobacco and asks what changed; Dina rejects "every single premise" and pitches an industry-wide time cap.
bullets: Jason: the settlement ranks behind only tobacco and ahead of BP; Facebook knew products were addictive, and Muse and character-based AI companions could be worse.

Dina (8 months at Meta after its board; mother of six daughters): the deal with 52 bipartisan attorneys general caps under-18s (not 16) at 2 hours a day, shuts the app at night, and blocks school-day notifications.
Meta offered more money and a 1-hour cap if **YouTube, TikTok and Snap** join — because kids just switch apps.

Chamath: for parents it's "whack-a-mole" since his five kids live on YouTube for school; he loved his son hitting the limit at dinner. Texas fans told Dina the cutoff hurts Instagram-driven football recruiting.

Sacks defends Meta: adults suing over a voluntary product plus AGs and trial lawyers is "a little bit of a shakedown"; parents, not government, should decide — but the new defaults are an improvement.
Chamath's warning: with RSI and a reward function of time, any app becomes an addiction engine ("Microsoft Word will keep you there for 9 hours if it can") unless companies set hard thresholds.

quote.text: Well, I totally disagree with basically every single premise in your question.

themes.watch: The settlement dollar figures in the captions are garbled; Dina says Jason's numbers were wrong.

themes.status: FIRST AMERICAN OPEN-SOURCE MODEL SHIPPED WEEKS AGO
themes.title: Glasses as the AI form factor, and Zuckerberg's case for distributing superintelligence
themes.lead: Dina says AI makes glasses sticky at last, and that Meta's answer to Dario's pacing essay is broad distribution, not restriction.
bullets: Chamath's challenge: Google Glass and Apple's VR became drawer relics — what's the repeat use case? Dina: music, calls, photos and video hands-free; Oakleys for extreme sports.
New features: conversation focus (hear only the person you're looking at) and live translation; the product took ~10 years of engineering, with Zuckerberg obsessing over weight and style.
Breakout use case: blind veterans at an Austin VFW (with Chris Stapleton, on 9/11) co-designed features; one called his son on his own for the first time.
Jason, a user since Google Glass: battery and fidelity finally work, unlike Siri — "time for people to reconsider." Meta has an exclusive partnership with EssilorLuxottica (Ray-Ban).
On Dario's essay (and an unconfirmed report that Zuckerberg said "go as fast as we can"): safety is paramount, and Alexandr Wang and Nat Friedman run the lab with a dedicated safety team.

Zuckerberg's view ("the future is for everyone"): with 3.6B daily users and 200M small businesses, spreading superintelligence makes society more stable; Meta shipped the first American open-source model a few weeks ago.

quote.text: The democratization of artificial intelligence will actually lead to a more stable society. That is just a fundamental belief that he has.
quote.cite: — Dina Powell McCormick, on Mark Zuckerberg

themes.watch: Dina listens to All-In on her Meta glasses — the hosts are friendly toward the product; Sacks notes a well-designed hit invites addiction lawsuits either way.

names.blurb: VR headset cited as a sticky-less face product; Chamath bought AirPods 5.

takeaways.title: Judge data-center deals by who pays for generation, grid and storm costs — Meta's Louisiana terms are the template to ask for.
Tie local AI-infrastructure tax windfalls to named beneficiaries (teachers, responders) in law, so residents see the dividend.
Consider paid, 4-5 week data-center trade programs as a fast route into $100K+ electrical and welding work.
Set cross-app screen limits yourself — single-platform caps just push kids to YouTube or TikTok.
Retest AI glasses if you wrote them off: translation, conversation focus and accessibility are the real use cases.
